claim: Col1a1 is expressed strongly in epicardial cells at all analyzed stages from E11.5 to P3.
source: We observed a strong expression of Col1a1 in epicardial cells at all analyzed stages (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA staining data shown in Figure 1A across multiple developmental stages

claim: Col1a1-positive cells are enriched at the boundary of the atrial and ventricular regions in E11.5 and E12.5 hearts, indicating their presence in the atrioventricular canal (AVC).
source: Inside the heart, we found Col1a1-positive cells enriched at the boundary of the atrial and ventricular regions in E11.5 and 12.5 hearts (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating their presence in the atrioventricular canal (AVC).
evidence: Supported by RNA staining data and anatomical localization shown in figures

claim: By E13.5 and E14.5, the AVC cells had developed into valve structures, and the valve interstitial cells highly expressed Col1a1.
source: By E13.5 and 14.5, the AVC cells had developed into valve structures, and the valve interstitial cells highly expressed Col1a1 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA staining data showing Col1a1 expression in valve structures at these stages

claim: A small proportion of Col1a1-positive cells were observed adjacent to the epicardium in the ventricles at E13.5 and E14.5.
source: In the ventricles, a small proportion of Col1a1-positive cells were observed adjacent to the epicardium.
evidence: Supported by RNA staining observations at these developmental stages

claim: Few Col1a1 signals were found in the atrium at E13.5 and E14.5.
source: In contrast, few Col1a1 signals were found in the atrium at this stage (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA staining data showing sparse Col1a1 expression in atrium

claim: At E15.5 and E16.5, both ventricles were filled with Col1a1-positive cells, but the middle of the ventricular septum remained devoid of such cells.
source: At E15.5 and 16.5, both ventricles were filled with Col1a1-positive cells, but the middle of the ventricular septum remained devoid of such cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA staining data showing spatial distribution of Col1a1-positive cells

claim: FBs were found in the atrium at E15.5 and E16.5, but the signal at the tips of both atrial chambers was sparser.
source: FBs were also found in the atrium, but the signal at the tips of both atrial chambers was sparser (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA staining data showing differential FB distribution in atrium

claim: The distribution of FBs at E17.5 and E18.5 was highly similar to that observed at E16.5.
source: The distribution of FBs at E17.5 and E18.5 was highly similar to that observed at E16.5 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparative RNA staining data across these stages

claim: Dense Col1a1 expression was found at the valves and in all four chambers at P0, P2, and P3.
source: Furthermore, we analyzed the Col1a1 signal in P0, P2, and P3 hearts and found dense Col1a1 expression at the valves and in all four chambers (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA staining data at postnatal stages

claim: FBs developed first in the AVC and valve, then at the ventricular wall and atrial, and last at the ventricular septum.
source: Specifically, we found that the FBs developed first in the AVC and valve, then at the ventricular wall and atrial, and last at the ventricular septum (Figure 1B).
evidence: Inferred from temporal and spatial analysis of Col1a1 expression across developmental stages

claim: Each FB was in contact with approximately one Vas_EC and four CMs at E17.5 and P3.
source: The quantification results showed that each FB was in contact with approximately one Vas_EC and four CMs at both stages (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of cell contacts from RNA staining data

claim: Cardiac FBs are physically close to CMs and ECs, likely facilitating signal communications that impact their development.
source: These results suggest that cardiac FBs are physically close to CMs and ECs, likely facilitating signal communications that impact their development.
evidence: Inferred from the observed physical proximity of these cell types

claim: Col1a1 is highly expressed in epicardial cells and FBs based on scRNA-seq data analysis.
source: Through the analysis of scRNA-seq data at 18 stages of developing hearts from CD1 mice, we investigated the expression of Col1a1 and observed high expression in epicardial cells and FBs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data analysis across 18 developmental stages

claim: Four distinct populations comprising 13 clusters were identified within cardiac FBs.
source: Subsequently, we reanalyzed the FBs and identified four distinct populations comprising 13 clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by unsupervised clustering analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: One group of FB cells highly expressed Hapln1, a marker gene associated with valves, indicating that these cells are valve interstitial cells.
source: Moreover, through differential gene expression analysis between the populations, we discovered that one group of cells highly expressed Hapln1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, D, E), a marker gene associated with valves. This indicates that these cells are valve interstitial cells.
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis and known marker gene associations

claim: A group of FB cells expressing Cdh5 and Tie1 may represent FBs derived from endothelial-derived cells (EDCs).
source: We also found another group of cells expressing Cdh5 and Tie1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, D, E), genes associated with the endothelial cell lineage. This suggests that these cells may represent FBs derived from EDCs.
evidence: Inferred from expression of endothelial lineage marker genes

claim: A group of FBs expressing Sox10 and Phox2b may originate from neural crest cells.
source: Additionally, we identified a third group of FBs expressing Sox10 and Phox2b (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, D, E), genes associated with the neural crest cell lineage. This suggests that these cells may originate from neural crest cells.
evidence: Inferred from expression of neural crest lineage marker genes

claim: The main population of FBs likely represents epicardial cell-derived FBs in the chambers, as they expressed Tcf21 and other marker genes.
source: Finally, the rest of the cells formed a main population that likely represents epicardial cell-derived FBs in the chambers, as they expressed Tcf21 and other marker genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, E).
evidence: Inferred from expression of epicardial lineage marker genes

claim: Each FB population consisted of cells in all three cell cycle phases, indicating active proliferation during the early stages.
source: Interestingly, further analysis of the cell cycle phases in these FBs revealed that each population consisted of cells in all three phases (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), indicating active proliferation during the early stages.
evidence: Supported by cell cycle phase analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Hapln1 is highly expressed in valves, and most of its signal overlapped with Dcn, suggesting its expression in valve interstitial cells.
source: Firstly, we stained Hapln1 together with Dcn, another Pan-FB marker gene. We found that Hapln1 was highly expressed in valves, and most of its signal overlapped with Dcn (Figure 1—figure supplement 3Fi), suggesting its expression in valve interstitial cells (FB-like cells in valves).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data showing co-localization

claim: A small cluster of cells expressing both Cdh5 and Col1a1 was observed, mostly located at the boundary of large vessels and ventricular chambers.
source: We also stained Cdh5 with Col1a1 and observed a small cluster of cells with the expression of both genes, mostly located at the boundary of large vessels and ventricular chambers (Figure 1—figure supplement 3Fii).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data showing co-expression and localization

claim: Sox10 and Col1a1 double-positive cells were identified in the outflow tract-derived large vessels.
source: Finally, we co-stained Sox10 and Col1a1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3Fiii). As previously reported (Ali et al., 2014), we identified double-positive cells in the outflow tract-derived large vessels (Figure 1—figure supplement 3Fiii_1).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data and previous literature

claim: Sox10 and Col1a1 double-positive cells were also observed in coronary vessels, suggesting that these cells may have a broader function than previously thought.
source: However, interestingly, we also observed their presence in coronary vessels (Figure 1—figure supplement 3Fiii_2), suggesting that these cells may have a broader function than previously thought.
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data showing unexpected localization

claim: Each cell type, except blood cells, had a similar number of interactions based on scRNA-seq data analysis.
source: By quantifying the number and strength of these interactions, we found that each cell type, except blood cells, had a similar number of interactions.
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: FB exhibited the highest interaction strength values compared to those of other cell types.
source: However, in terms of interaction strength, FB exhibited the highest values compared to those of other cell types (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of cell-cell interaction strength from scRNA-seq data

claim: The collagen pathway was the predominant pathway in both FB-VenCM and FB-VasEC interactions.
source: Next, we analyzed the signaling pathways secreted from FB to ventricular cardiomyocytes (Ven_CM) and Vas_EC. Interestingly, we found that the collagen pathway was the predominant pathway in both FB-VenCM and FB-VasEC interactions (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: In addition to collagen, other signaling molecules such as laminin, Ptn, MK, Fn1, and Thbs, which are mostly extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, are secreted by FB to function in Ven_CM and Vas_EC.
source: In addition to collagen, we identified other signaling molecules such as laminin, Ptn, MK, Fn1, and Thbs, which are mostly extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, as being secreted by FB to function in Ven_CM and Vas_EC (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by signaling pathway analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: More collagen ligand-receptor interaction pairs were found in FB-VasEC than in FB-VenCM.
source: Within the collagen pathway, we further analyzed the detailed ligand-receptor interactions and found more interaction pairs in FB-VasEC than in FB-VenCM.
evidence: Supported by detailed ligand-receptor interaction analysis

claim: Some collagen interactions were shared between FB-VenCM and FB-VasEC, but most were distinct.
source: Some interactions were shared between the two cell types, but most were distinct (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of ligand-receptor interactions

claim: All the shared collagen types have been previously studied and found to play a crucial role in heart development, primarily by regulating AVC and vasculature development.
source: Consistently, all the shared collagen types have been previously studied and found to play a crucial role in heart development, primarily by regulating AVC and vasculature development (Kruithof et al., 2007; Lincoln et al., 2004; Lincoln et al., 2006; van der Kooi et al., 2006; Lockhart et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations

claim: Strong collagen signals were observed in the epicardium at all analyzed stages (E11.5, E14.5, E16.5, and P3).
source: Consistent with Col1a1 expression, we observed strong collagen signals in the epicardium at all analyzed stages (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by CHP staining data across multiple developmental stages

claim: At E11.5, collagen was observed in both AVC and ventricular chambers.
source: Interestingly, at E11.5, we observed collagen in both AVC and ventricular chambers.
evidence: Supported by CHP staining data at E11.5

claim: The collagen observed at E11.5 in ventricular chambers is likely derived from other cell types, such as endocardial endothelial cells, since FBs in the chambers have not developed yet at this stage.
source: Given that FBs in the chambers have not developed yet at this stage, the observed collagen is likely derived from other cell types, such as endocardial endothelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of FBs in chambers at E11.5 and presence of collagen

claim: At E14.5, a strong collagen signal was observed in the ventricular free walls, while the signal in the ventricular septum and atrium was relatively weaker.
source: At E14.5, we observed a strong collagen signal in the ventricular free walls, while the signal in the ventricular septum and atrium was relatively weaker.
evidence: Supported by CHP staining data at E14.5

claim: At E16.5, the collagen signal became brighter and denser throughout the heart, including the ventricular free wall, septum, and atrium.
source: At E16.5, the collagen signal became brighter and denser throughout the heart, including the ventricular free wall, septum, and atrium.
evidence: Supported by CHP staining data at E16.5

claim: The collagen distribution at E16.5 was slightly broader compared to the fibroblast distribution at the same stage.
source: This distribution was slightly broader compared to the fibroblast distribution at the same stage (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of collagen staining and FB marker expression

claim: By P3, the collagen signal had further increased and formed stripe patterns.
source: By P3, the collagen signal had further increased and formed stripe patterns (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by CHP staining data at P3

claim: The progression of collagen accumulation largely coincided with the development of FBs.
source: In summary, we found that the progression of collagen accumulation largely coincided with the development of FBs.
evidence: Inferred from temporal correlation between collagen deposition and FB development

claim: Five groups of ECM genes displayed stage or chamber-specific expression in both CD1 and C57BL/6 datasets.
source: Interestingly, we identified five groups of ECM genes that displayed stage or chamber-specific expression in both datasets (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4, Supplementary file 3 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of ECM gene expression in scRNA-seq data

claim: Group 1 (G1) ECM genes were highly expressed at stages before E14.5 and include signaling molecules such as Slit2 and Wnt5a, and collagen genes such as Col13a1 and Col26a1.
source: Specifically, we found one group of genes (G1) that was highly expressed at stages before E14.5. This gene group includes signaling molecules such as Slit2 and Wnt5a, and collagen genes such as Col13a1 and Col26a1 (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: Supported by temporal expression analysis of ECM genes in scRNA-seq data

claim: Group 2 (G2) ECM genes were mainly expressed in the LV and RV from E14.5 onwards with a significant increase at the neonatal stage, including collagen genes such as Col5a1, Col6a1, and Col6a2, and metalloproteinase genes such as Adamts13 and Adamts14.
source: We found the second group of genes (G2) was mainly expressed in the LV and RV from E14.5 onwards with a significant increase at the neonatal stage. This gene group includes collagen genes such as Col5a1, Col6a1, and Col6a2, and metalloproteinase genes such as Adamts13 and Adamts14.
evidence: Supported by temporal and spatial expression analysis of ECM genes in scRNA-seq data

claim: Group 3 (G3) ECM genes were highly expressed in the LA and RA at most stages, including Col12a1, Adamts1, Adamts4, and Fn1.
source: Additionally, we identified that the third group of genes was highly expressed in the LA and RA at most stages, which includes Col12a1, Adamts1, and Adamts4. Interestingly, Fn1 also exists in this group, suggesting that it has an important function in atrial FB development.
evidence: Supported by chamber-specific expression analysis of ECM genes in scRNA-seq data

claim: Group 4 (G4) ECM genes were preferentially expressed in LA, LV, and RV (but not RA) mainly at late neonatal stages after P5, including Col4a4, Col4a5, Col4a6, and Ntn4.
source: Furthermore, we found the fourth group of genes was preferentially expressed in the other three chambers than the RA and was mainly expressed at late neonatal stages after P5 in certain chambers. This group of genes includes Col4a4, Col4a5, Col4a6, and Ntn4.
evidence: Supported by temporal and chamber-specific expression analysis of ECM genes in scRNA-seq data

claim: Group 5 (G5) ECM genes displayed universal expression in all four chambers at most stages, including Col1a1, Col1a2, and Postn, which are ubiquitously expressed extracellular matrix genes.
source: Finally, we identified the fifth group of genes displayed universal expression in all four chambers at most stages. This gene group includes Col1a1, Col1a2, and Postn, which are the ubiquitously expressed extracellular matrix genes (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis showing consistent expression across chambers and stages

claim: Collagen pathway interactions were enriched at most analyzed stages between FB and Ven_CM or Vas_EC.
source: Additionally, we analyzed the ligand-receptor interactions between FB and Ven_CM or Vas_EC at each stage. We found collagen pathway interactions were also enriched at most analyzed stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A, B, Supplementary file 5 and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by stage-specific ligand-receptor interaction analysis

claim: Strong interactions were identified between FB and other cardiac cell types in human embryonic hearts.
source: Lastly, we analyzed the signaling interactions among human cardiac cells using a human embryonic heart scRNA-seq dataset (Asp et al., 2019). Consistent with the mouse analysis results, we identified strong interactions between FB and other cardiac cell types (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of human scRNA-seq data

claim: Collagen was the most enriched pathway in FB-VasEC interactions in human embryonic hearts.
source: Additionally, we found collagen to be the most enriched pathway in FB-VasEC interactions.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis of human scRNA-seq data

claim: The collagen pathway was not observed among the top enriched pathways in FB-VenCM interactions in human embryonic hearts.
source: However, interestingly, we did not observe the collagen pathway among the top enriched pathways in FB-VenCM interactions (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis of human scRNA-seq data

claim: The mechanism underlying FB regulation of heart development is partially similar in both mice and humans.
source: These results suggest a partially similar mechanism underlying FB regulation of heart development in both mice and humans.
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis of mouse and human scRNA-seq data showing both similarities and differences

claim: Postn was highly expressed in FBs and mural cells, and among FBs, Postn was expressed in all subpopulations.
source: We observed that Postn was highly expressed in FBs and mural cells. Among FBs, Postn was expressed in all subpopulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ai).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data analysis of Postn expression

claim: Pdgfra was specifically expressed in FBs, although its expression was relatively lower than Postn, especially in postnatal staged atrial cells.
source: On the other hand, Pdgfra was specifically expressed in FBs, although its expression was relatively lower than Postn, especially in postnatal staged atrial cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Aii).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data analysis of Pdgfra expression

claim: Postn-CreER mice showed low labeling efficiency with only a small proportion of GFP-positive cells in the valves and septum at E17.5 after tamoxifen administration at E13.5.
source: To evaluate their efficiency in labeling FBs, we bred Postn-CreER mice with Rosa-mTmG reporter mice and administered tamoxifen (200 µg/g) to pregnant mice at E13.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Bi). We collected the hearts at E17.5 and observed only a small proportion of GFP-positive cells in the valves and septum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Bii), suggesting a low labeling efficiency from the Postn-CreER mice.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing experiments using Postn-CreER; Rosa-mTmG mice

claim: Pdgfra-CreER; Rosa-mTmG mice showed efficient labeling with a significant proportion of GFP-positive cells in both the valves and heart chambers.
source: In contrast, we conducted the same experiments using Pdgfra-CreER mice and observed a significant proportion of GFP-positive cells in both the valves and heart chambers (Figure 3A). These results demonstrate the efficient labeling capability of the Pdgfra-CreER; Rosa-mTmG mice.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing experiments using Pdgfra-CreER; Rosa-mTmG mice

claim: All embryos with ablated FBs (Pdgfra-CreER+/-; Rosa-DTA+/-) perished after tamoxifen administration at E10.5, while control embryos remained unaffected.
source: Initially, we crossed floxed Rosa-DTA mice with Pdgfra-CreER mice and administered tamoxifen to pregnant female mice at E10.5. After 3 days, we harvested the embryos and observed that all the embryos with ablated FBs (Pdgfra-CreER+/-; Rosa-DTA+/-) had perished, while the control embryos remained unaffected.
evidence: Supported by FB ablation experiments at E10.5

claim: FBs play an essential role in early-stage embryo development.
source: This outcome indicates an essential role for FBs in early-stage embryo development.
evidence: Inferred from the lethality observed when FBs are ablated at E10.5

claim: Ablated embryos at E16.5 (after tamoxifen treatment at E13.5) exhibited smaller sizes compared to control embryos, although the size of the ablated hearts did not significantly differ from that of the control hearts.
source: Subsequently, we administered tamoxifen to the female mice from the breeding pair at E13.5 and collected the embryonic hearts at E16.5 (Figure 3B). Our findings revealed that the ablated embryos exhibited smaller sizes compared to the control embryos, although the size of the ablated hearts did not significantly differ from that of the control hearts (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis of ablated and control embryos and hearts

claim: A significantly higher number of TUNEL-positive dots were observed in the valve and chamber regions of the ablated hearts compared to the control hearts at E16.5.
source: Additionally, we conducted TUNEL analysis to assess cell death in both control and ablated hearts and observed a significantly higher number of TUNEL-positive dots in the valve and chamber regions of the ablated hearts compared to the control hearts, confirming the successful ablation of FBs in the experimental hearts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining data confirming cell death in ablated hearts

claim: A reduction in endothelial cell density was observed in the ablated hearts at E16.5, as indicated by the CD31 staining signal.
source: However, we observed a reduction in endothelial cell density in the ablated hearts, as indicated by the CD31 staining signal (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by CD31 immunofluorescence staining data

claim: Ablated hearts at E16.5 exhibited a thinner left ventricular (LV) compact myocardium compared to control hearts, while the thickness of the LV trabecular myocardium remained similar.
source: Additionally, we measured the thickness of the compact and trabecular myocardium (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C). Our observations revealed that, compared to the control hearts, the ablated hearts exhibited a thinner left ventricular (LV) compact myocardium, while the thickness of the LV trabecular myocardium remained similar.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of myocardium thickness

claim: An elevated ratio of LV trabecular to compact myocardium was noted in the ablated hearts compared to the control hearts at E16.5.
source: Furthermore, we noted an elevated ratio of LV trabecular to compact myocardium in the ablated hearts compared to the control hearts (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of myocardium thickness ratios

claim: No similar differences in myocardium thickness were observed in the right ventricle (RV) at E16.5.
source: However, no similar differences were observed in the right ventricle (RV).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements showing no significant differences in RV

claim: A reduction in pHH3-positive cells was observed in the ventricular region, but not in the atrial region, of the ablated hearts compared to the control hearts at E16.5.
source: Finally, we examined cell proliferation post-ablation using pHH3 staining. We observed a reduction in pHH3-positive cells in the ventricular region, but not in the atrial region, of the ablated hearts compared to the control hearts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by pHH3 immunofluorescence staining data

claim: Cell proliferation in the ventricle was impaired following FB ablation at E13.5.
source: These results suggest that cell proliferation in the ventricle was impaired following FB ablation.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in pHH3-positive cells in ablated ventricles

claim: No obvious differences in the size of the embryos and hearts were observed between the ablated group and the control group at E18.5 after one dose of tamoxifen treatment at E15.5.
source: Next, we performed ablation at late embryonic stages by treating the pregnant mice with tamoxifen at E15.5 and harvested the embryos at E18.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A). We did not observe obvious differences in the size of the embryos and hearts between the ablated group and the control group (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis of ablated and control embryos and hearts

claim: CD31 staining revealed large holes in the ablated atrium but not in the ablated ventricles or control hearts at E18.5 after one dose of tamoxifen treatment at E15.5.
source: However, the CD31 staining of heart sections revealed large holes in the ablated atrium but not in the ablated ventricles or control hearts (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by CD31 immunofluorescence staining data

claim: A thinner LV compact myocardium was observed in ablated hearts at E18.5 after one dose of tamoxifen treatment at E15.5.
source: Additionally, quantification of the compact and trabecular myocardium thickness in the LV and RV revealed a thinner LV compact myocardium (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of myocardium thickness

claim: The ratio of trabecular to compact myocardium thickness was increased in the RV but not in the LV of the ablated hearts at E18.5 after one dose of tamoxifen treatment at E15.5.
source: We also calculated the ratio of trabecular to compact myocardium thickness in the LV and RV and found that the ratio was increased in the RV but not in the LV of the ablated hearts compared to control hearts (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of myocardium thickness ratios

claim: Both the LV and RV of the ablated hearts have subtle defects at E18.5 after one dose of tamoxifen treatment at E15.5.
source: These results indicated that both the LV and RV of the ablated hearts have subtle defects.
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in myocardium thickness and ratios

claim: No significant differences in cell proliferation were found between the ablated and control ventricles at E18.5 after one dose of tamoxifen treatment at E15.5.
source: Moreover, we analyzed cell proliferation by staining pHH3 and found no significant differences between the ablated and control ventricles (Figure 3—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: Supported by pHH3 immunofluorescence staining data

claim: Both the ablated embryos and their hearts were notably smaller in size compared to the controls at E18.5 after three consecutive days of tamoxifen treatment from E15.5 to E17.5.
source: Given that the animals did not show obvious morphological changes after one dose of tamoxifen treatment, we increased the tamoxifen treatment to three consecutive days, ranging from E15.5 to E17.5 (Figure 3E). We harvested the embryos at E18.5 and found that both the ablated embryos and their hearts were notably smaller in size compared to the controls (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis of ablated and control embryos and hearts

claim: The ablated hearts lost almost all of their Col1a1 signal in the four chambers at E18.5 after three doses of tamoxifen treatments, indicating a high ablation efficiency.
source: Next, to confirm the ablation efficiency, we analyzed Col1a1 expression with RNA staining and found that the ablated hearts lost almost all of their Col1a1 signal in the four chambers (Figure 3—figure supplement 4G), indicating a high ablation efficiency with three doses of tamoxifen treatments.
evidence: Supported by RNA staining data showing loss of Col1a1 expression

claim: The valves in the ablated hearts were not severely affected at E18.5 after three doses of tamoxifen treatments.
source: We further analyzed their valve structures and observed that the valves in the ablated hearts were not severely affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis of valve structures

claim: The ablated hearts exhibited a significantly lower endothelial cell density at E18.5 after three doses of tamoxifen treatments.
source: Moreover, by conducting a staining analysis of CD31 in the control and ablated heart sections, we discovered that the ablated hearts exhibited a significantly lower endothelial cell density (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by CD31 immunofluorescence staining data

claim: A significant reduction in both LV compact and trabecular myocardium thickness was observed in the ablated hearts compared to control hearts at E18.5 after three doses of tamoxifen treatments.
source: Further quantification of the LV compact and trabecular myocardium thickness showed a significant reduction in the ablated hearts compared to control hearts (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of myocardium thickness

claim: The ratio of trabecular to compact myocardium thickness in the LV did not differ between the control and ablated hearts at E18.5 after three doses of tamoxifen treatments, indicating a proportional reduction in both compact and trabecular myocardium thickness in the ablated hearts.
source: However, interestingly, the ratio of trabecular to compact myocardium thickness in the LV did not differ between the control and ablated hearts, indicating a proportional reduction in both compact and trabecular myocardium thickness in the ablated hearts.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of myocardium thickness ratios

claim: The ablated ventricles had less pHH3 signal than the control ventricles at E18.5 after three doses of tamoxifen treatments, indicating impaired cell proliferation in the ventricles following FB ablation.
source: Finally, we found that the ablated ventricles had less pHH3 signal than the control ventricles (Figure 3—figure supplement 4F), indicating impaired cell proliferation in the ventricles following FB ablation.
evidence: Supported by pHH3 immunofluorescence staining data

claim: FB plays an important role in embryonic heart development at all the analyzed stages.
source: These results together indicated that FB plays an important role in embryonic heart development at all the analyzed stages.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple defects observed across different ablation time points

claim: Eight cell types were identified in the scRNA-seq analysis: Atrial_CM, Ven_CM, Vas_EC, Endo_EC, Mural_cell, FB, Epicardial cell, and Immune cell.
source: In total, we identified eight cell types: Atrial_CM, Ven_CM, Vas_EC, Endo_EC, Mural_cell, FB, Epicardial cell, and Immune cell, along with three cell cycle phases (G1, S, G2M) in each cell type (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by unsupervised clustering analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: The percentage of FB was significantly reduced in the ablated hearts at both E16.5 and E18.5, indicating effective ablation.
source: We further quantified the percentages of each cell type across conditions and found that the percentage of FB was significantly reduced in the ablated hearts at both stages, indicating effective ablation.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of cell type proportions in scRNA-seq data

claim: A reduction in mural cells was observed in the ablated hearts at both E16.5 and E18.5.
source: Interestingly, we also observed a reduction in mural cells in the ablated hearts at both stages (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of cell type proportions in scRNA-seq data

claim: Four FB subpopulations were identified: valve fibroblasts (valve-fb), neural crest-derived fibroblasts (Neural_crest_fb), chamber-derived main fibroblasts (main_fb), and dying fibroblasts (dying_fb).
source: By analyzing the expression of cardiac lineage genes, cell cycle phases, and sample sources, we identified four FB subpopulations (Figure 4E). Specifically, we identified a group of valve fibroblasts (valve-fb) expressing valve mesenchymal cell genes such as Hapln1, a group of neural crest-derived fibroblasts (Neural_crest_fb) expressing Sox10, and a group of chamber-derived main fibroblasts (main_fb) expressing Wt1 and Tcf21 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by clustering and marker gene expression analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Dying fibroblasts (dying_fb) were exclusively derived from the ablated samples and expressed cell death-related genes.
source: In contrast, we identified another group of cells exclusively derived from the ablated samples, which expressed cell death-related genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C). We named this group dying fibroblasts (dying_fb).
evidence: Supported by clustering and gene expression analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: The ablated samples had slightly higher percentages of Ven_CM cells in the G1 phase compared to control samples.
source: We quantified the proportions of cells at each cell cycle phase and found that the ablated samples had slightly higher percentages of cells in the G1 phase compared to control samples (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle phase analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Ablated Ven_CMs upregulated genes associated with heart development and cell proliferation at E16.5.
source: Gene ontology analysis of the upregulated genes in the ablated CMs showed enrichment in various pathways, including heart development, sarcomere organization, heart tube morphogenesis, and cell proliferation.
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression and gene ontology analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Ablated Ven_CMs downregulated genes related to cell maturation, including those involved in mitochondrial function and cell metabolism at E16.5.
source: In contrast, the downregulated genes were enriched in pathways related to chaperone-dependent protein folding, mitochondrial membrane permeability, fatty acid import, and mitochondrial ATP transmembrane transport (Figure 4I). These results indicated that ablated Ven_CMs upregulated genes associated with heart development and cell proliferation while downregulating genes related to cell maturation, including those involved in mitochondrial function and cell metabolism.
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression and gene ontology analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Vas_EC in ablated samples exhibited upregulated genes primarily involved in immune response pathways at E16.5.
source: However, through further differential expression analysis, we identified a group of genes with upregulated expression in the ablated samples (Figure 4K, Supplementary file 9). Gene ontology analysis of these genes revealed that they were primarily involved in immune response pathways, including type I and II interferon production, interleukin-27-mediated pathways, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and cellular responses to exogenous dsRNA (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression and gene ontology analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Vas_EC exhibits a strong immune response following FB ablation.
source: These results suggest that Vas_EC exhibits a strong immune response following FB ablation.
evidence: Inferred from the upregulation of immune response genes in ablated Vas_EC

claim: The collagen pathway consistently ranked at the top in signaling pathways between main_fb and Vas_EC or Ven_CM in both control and ablated samples.
source: Through the analysis of signaling pathways between main_fb and Vas_EC or Ven_CM, we found that the collagen pathway consistently ranked at the top in both control and ablated samples (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Collagen deposition was dramatically reduced in both the septum and ventricular wall of the ablated hearts compared to the control hearts.
source: We then stained for collagen levels using collagen hybridizing peptide and observed that collagen deposition was dramatically reduced in both the septum and ventricular wall of the ablated hearts compared to the control hearts (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by CHP staining data

claim: The collagen pathway, which has four different collagen ligands on the list, emerged as a major regulator of differentially expressed genes in control and ablated Ven_CM.
source: Moreover, by analyzing the scRNA-seq data, we predicted the signaling ligands that may regulate the differentially expressed genes in control and ablated Ven_CM. Interestingly, the collagen pathway, which has four different collagen ligands on the list, emerged as a major regulator of these genes (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by NicheNet regulatory analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: In addition to collagens, other ligands such as TGF-beta, IGF, and BMP were derived from FB and regulate the expression of differentially expressed genes in control and ablated Ven_CMs.
source: In addition to collagens, we also identified other ligands, such as TGF-beta, IGF, and BMP, which were derived from FB and regulate the expression of differentially expressed genes in control and ablated Ven_CMs (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by NicheNet regulatory analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Several signaling molecules including the DTA pathway-related signal Hbegf, the inflammation-associated signal Il33, Wnt ligands (Wnt11, Wnt4, and Wnt5b), and collagen Col4a6 were predicted as ligands in FB that regulate the differentially expressed genes in Vas_EC.
source: Furthermore, we predicted the ligands in FB that regulate the differentially expressed genes in Vas_EC and identified several signaling molecules. These included the DTA pathway-related signal Hbegf, the inflammation-associated signal Il33, Wnt ligands (Wnt11, Wnt4, and Wnt5b), and collagen Col4a6 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by NicheNet regulatory analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Dying_fb downregulated certain signaling pathways, such as the IGF pathway, EphA pathway, Tenascin pathway, and collagen pathway compared to normal main_fb and valve_like_fb.
source: Finally, we predicted the signals from the dying_fb cells. Compared to normal main_fb and valve_like_fb, the dying_fb downregulated certain signaling pathways, such as the IGF pathway, EphA pathway, Tenascin pathway, and collagen pathway (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by CellChat pathway analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Dying_fb upregulated several signaling pathways, including the EGF pathway, BMP pathway, VEGF pathway, and FGF pathway.
source: Interestingly, they also upregulated several signaling pathways, including the EGF pathway, BMP pathway, VEGF pathway, and FGF pathway (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by CellChat pathway analysis of scRNA-seq data

claim: Collagen and other ECM proteins are essential structural components and their roles as structural proteins in heart development are critical and contribute to the heart phenotype observed in the ablated hearts.
source: Additionally, collagen and other ECM proteins are essential structural components. Their roles as structural proteins in heart development are critical and contribute to the heart phenotype observed in the ablated hearts.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ECM protein functions

claim: No obvious differences were observed between the ablated and control hearts at P4 after tamoxifen treatment at P1.
source: Next, we assessed the FB function at neonatal stage. We treated the mice with tamoxifen at P1 and harvested them at P4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). We did not observe any obvious differences between the ablated and control hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), consistent with a recent study that used the same strategy to ablate FBs during a similar time period (Kuwabara et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and consistent with published literature

claim: CD31 staining of heart sections revealed defects in the atrium, which had a thinner and segmented atrial wall at P4 after tamoxifen treatment at P1.
source: However, CD31 staining of heart sections revealed defects in the atrium, which had a thinner and segmented atrial wall (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by CD31 immunofluorescence staining data

claim: No differences in compact and trabecular myocardium thickness were observed between control and ablated hearts in both the LV and RV at P4 after one dose of tamoxifen treatment at P1.
source: We further quantified the compact and trabecular myocardium in both the LV and RV but did not observe differences between control and ablated hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of myocardium thickness

claim: No differences in the ratio of trabecular to compact myocardium thickness were found between control and ablated hearts in the LV and RV at P4 after one dose of tamoxifen treatment at P1.
source: We also did not find differences in the ratio of trabecular to compact myocardium thickness between control and ablated hearts in the LV and RV (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of myocardium thickness ratios

claim: No differences in cell proliferation were observed between control and ablated hearts at P4 after one dose of tamoxifen treatment at P1.
source: Finally, we analyzed cell proliferation by staining pHH3 and did not observe differences between the two conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by pHH3 immunofluorescence staining data

claim: The heart morphology and size did not reveal obvious differences between control and ablated groups at P4 after three doses of tamoxifen treatment from P1 to P3.
source: Next, we increased the tamoxifen treatments to three times, ranging from P1 to P3, and collected hearts at P4 (Figure 6A). The heart morphology and size did not reveal obvious differences between control and ablated groups (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis of hearts

claim: A reduction in endothelial cell density was observed in the ablated hearts when compared to the control hearts at P4 after three doses of tamoxifen treatment.
source: The CD31 staining revealed a reduction in endothelial cell density in the ablated hearts when compared to the control hearts (Figure 6C). These reductions in both LV and RV were further confirmed through quantifications (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by CD31 immunofluorescence staining and quantification

claim: No apparent defects and cell proliferation changes were observed in ablated hearts with three days of tamoxifen treatments at P4.
source: Finally, we quantified the chamber thickness and cell proliferation. Similar to hearts treated with one dose of tamoxifen, we observed no apparent defects and cell proliferation changes in ablated hearts with three days of tamoxifen treatments (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of chamber thickness and pHH3 staining

claim: The ablated hearts at P4 had a sparser collagen signal and lost most of the stripe pattern in the septum compared to the control hearts, but a significant amount of stripe-patterned collagen was still observed in the ventricular free wall.
source: Furthermore, we stained the P4 hearts for collagen depositions. We observed that the ablated hearts had a sparser collagen signal and lost most of the stripe pattern in the septum compared to the control hearts. However, a significant amount of stripe-patterned collagen was still observed in the ventricular free wall, although the overall signal was sparser (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by CHP staining data

claim: The collagens observed in the ventricular free wall at P4 were likely derived from FBs before ablation.
source: These collagens were likely derived from FBs before ablation.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of ablation and collagen deposition

claim: Approximately two-thirds of the ablated mice had perished before P17 after tamoxifen administration from P3 to P5.
source: Lastly, we conducted a long-term analysis by administering tamoxifen to the mice from P3 to P5 and harvesting them at P17 or P18 (Figure 6F). We observed that approximately two-thirds of the ablated mice had perished before P17 (Figure 6G), and the surviving mice were significantly smaller than the control mice.
evidence: Supported by survival analysis and morphological observations

claim: The surviving ablated mice at P17 were significantly smaller than the control mice.
source: We observed that approximately two-thirds of the ablated mice had perished before P17 (Figure 6G), and the surviving mice were significantly smaller than the control mice.
evidence: Supported by morphological observations and measurements

claim: Ablated mice at P17 had reduced heart rates and body weights, but a similar heart-to-body ratio compared to controls.
source: Quantification revealed reduced heart rates and body weights, but a similar heart-to-body ratio in the ablated mice compared to controls (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements

claim: Ablated mice at P17 had reduced organ sizes, including smaller hearts, lungs, brains, kidneys, and livers.
source: A detailed examination of the major tissues showed reduced organ sizes in the ablated mice, including smaller hearts, lungs, brains, kidneys, and livers (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis of multiple organs

claim: Heart function, including ejection fraction (EF) and fractional shortening (FS), was not reduced in the ablated mice compared to controls at P17.
source: Additionally, we assessed mouse heart function using echocardiography before sacrificing them. Interestingly, we found that heart function, including ejection fraction (EF) and fractional shortening (FS), was not reduced in the ablated mice compared to controls (Figure 6H, I).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements

claim: No clear reduction or pattern change in collagen levels was observed in the ablated hearts at P17-P18.
source: Furthermore, we evaluated collagen levels in the ablated hearts and did not observe a clear reduction or pattern change (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by CHP staining data at P17-P18

claim: There may be potential collagen expression compensation at later stages after FB ablation.
source: This finding contrasts with our observations at P4 (Figure 6E) and suggests potential collagen expression compensation at later stages.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in collagen levels between P4 and P17-P18

claim: The lungs of the ablated mice exhibited reduced collagen levels and larger empty spaces compared to the controls at P18.
source: In contrast, we found that the lungs of the ablated mice exhibited reduced collagen levels and larger empty spaces compared to the controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by collagen staining of lung tissue

claim: FBs play a crucial role in the growth of multiple tissues during the neonatal phase.
source: These findings suggest that FBs play a crucial role in the growth of multiple tissues during the neonatal phase.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced organ sizes and tissue defects observed in ablated mice

claim: FB is one of the most abundant cardiac cell types and plays important roles in normal heart function and pathological heart remodeling at the adult stage.
source: Fibroblast (FB) is one of the most abundant cardiac cell types and plays important roles in normal heart function and pathological heart remodeling at the adult stage (Hall et al., 2021; Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017).
evidence: Supported by literature citations

claim: The FB composition in the heart has been analyzed with multiple approaches such as flow cytometry, with a focus on the left ventricle.
source: The FB composition in the heart has been analyzed with multiple approaches such as flow cytometry, with a focus on the left ventricle (Zhou and Pu, 2016; Pinto et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by literature citations

claim: The heart in mice starts to develop into a four-chambered structure at E9.5.
source: The heart in mice starts to develop into a four-chambered structure at E9.5.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mouse heart development

claim: The atrial and ventricular chambers are connected by the atrioventricular canal (AVC), a transient structure that develops into the septum and valve cells.
source: The atrial and ventricular chambers are connected by the atrioventricular canal (AVC), a transient structure that develops into the septum and valve cells (de Vlaming et al., 2012; O'Donnell and Yutzey, 2020).
evidence: Supported by literature citations

claim: The main FB population does not develop until E13.5.
source: Although the main FB population does not develop until E13.5 (Tallquist, 2020), FB-like cells with the expression of Col1a1 and other FB genes start to develop in the AVC at E9.5 (O'Donnell and Yutzey, 2020).
evidence: Supported by literature citations

claim: FB-like cells with the expression of Col1a1 and other FB genes start to develop in the AVC at E9.5.
source: Although the main FB population does not develop until E13.5 (Tallquist, 2020), FB-like cells with the expression of Col1a1 and other FB genes start to develop in the AVC at E9.5 (O'Donnell and Yutzey, 2020).
evidence: Supported by literature citations

claim: Vas_EC developed at about the same time as FB, while CM developed before the appearance of FB at the chambers.
source: CM and Vas_EC are the other two major cell types in the heart. Vas_EC developed at about the same time as FB, while CM developed before the appearance of FB at the chambers.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cardiac cell development

claim: FB has been shown to couple with CM through gap junctions and promote their maturation in human three-dimensional micro-tissue consisting of FB, CM, and EC.
source: FB has been shown to couple with CM through gap junctions and promote their maturation in human three-dimensional micro-tissue consisting of FB, CM, and EC (Giacomelli et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by literature citation

claim: In mice, epicardium-derived cells, mostly FBs, have been reported to serve as guidepost cells by secreting the chemokine Slit2, guiding Vas_EC to the correct anatomical locations and promoting their maturation.
source: In mice, epicardium-derived cells, mostly FBs, have been reported to serve as guidepost cells by secreting the chemokine Slit2, guiding Vas_EC to the correct anatomical locations and promoting their maturation (Quijada et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by literature citation

claim: The DTA system has been used in mice to ablate cardiac progenitor cells and cardiomyocytes at early developmental stages.
source: The DTA system has been used in mice to ablate cardiac progenitor cells and cardiomyocytes at early developmental stages (Sturzu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by literature citation

claim: A group of proliferating FBs with the expression of Postn was identified in neonatal hearts, and elimination of this cell population using the DTA ablation system showed its importance in promoting cardiomyocyte maturation.
source: Recently, a group of proliferating FBs with the expression of Postn was identified in neonatal hearts. Further elimination of this cell population using the DTA ablation system showed its importance in promoting cardiomyocyte maturation (Hortells et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by literature citation

claim: The DTA system has been used to ablate FBs at the adult stage to assess their function in adverse cardiac remodeling.
source: Additionally, the DTA system has been used to ablate FBs at the adult stage to assess their function in adverse cardiac remodeling (Kuwabara et al., 2022a; Kaur et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by literature citations

claim: One of the major functions of FB is to synthesize and secrete extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, which influence the behavior of other cell lineages.
source: One of the major functions of FB is to synthesize and secrete extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, which influence the behavior of other cell lineages (Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017; Ivey and Tallquist, 2016).
evidence: Supported by literature citations

claim: Collagen has 28 genes in vertebrates.
source: For example, collagen has 28 genes in vertebrates (Frantz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by literature citation

claim: Hyaluronan and proteoglycan link protein 1 (Hapln1) is critical in regulating myocardial compaction and heart regeneration in zebrafish.
source: For instance, hyaluronan and proteoglycan link protein 1 (Hapln1) is critical in regulating myocardial compaction and heart regeneration in zebrafish (Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by literature citation

claim: ECM has been found to regulate mouse CM proliferation through β1-integrin signaling in a cell co-culture assay.
source: ECM has also been found to regulate mouse CM proliferation through β1-integrin signaling in a cell co-culture assay (Ieda et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by literature citation

claim: Collagen has been shown to be essential for heart regeneration in adult zebrafish and mice.
source: Moreover, collagen has been shown to be essential for heart regeneration in adult zebrafish and mice (Simões et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by literature citation
